title: Given the dimensions of a chain of matrices, find the minimum number of scalar multiplications needed to compute the product, choosing the best parenthesization.
shortTitle: Matrix Chain Multiplication — interval DP for minimum multiplications

s1_definition.profdef: Interval DP where dp[i][j] is the minimum scalar multiplications to multiply matrices i through j. Split at k: dp[i][j] = min over k of dp[i][k] + dp[k+1][j] + p[i−1]·p[k]·p[j], where p is the dimension array. Time O(n³), space O(n²).
s1_definition.analogy: A risk engine at National Bank of India multiplies a chain of covariance matrices, and the order of multiplication drastically changes the arithmetic cost even though the result is the same. It tries every split point to find the cheapest way to group the multiplications.
s1_definition.oneliner: Split the chain at k; cost = left + right + p[i−1]·p[k]·p[j]; take the minimum.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Interval DP where dp[i][j] is the minimum scalar multiplications to multiply matrices i through j. Split at k: dp[i][j] = min over k of dp[i][k] + dp[k+1][j] + p[i−1]·p[k]·p[j], where p is the dimension array. Time O(n³), space O(n²).

**In simple words (banking analogy):** A risk engine at National Bank of India multiplies a chain of covariance matrices, and the order of multiplication drastically changes the arithmetic cost even though the result is the same. It tries every split point to find the cheapest way to group the multiplications.

**One line to remember:** Split the chain at k; cost = left + right + p[i−1]·p[k]·p[j]; take the minimum.

sections.s2_technical:
Matrix multiplication is associative, so the result is the same regardless of grouping, but the cost is not. If a matrix is a by b and the next is b by c, multiplying them costs a times b times c scalar multiplications. With dimensions stored in an array p, matrix i has dimensions p[i−1] by p[i].

Define dp[i][j] as the minimum cost to multiply the subchain from i to j. For every split point k between i and j, the cost is the cost of the left group dp[i][k], plus the right group dp[k+1][j], plus the cost of multiplying the two resulting matrices, which is p[i−1] times p[k] times p[j]. For example: `dp[i][j] = Math.min(dp[i][j], dp[i][k] + dp[k+1][j] + p[i-1]*p[k]*p[j]);`. The diagonal dp[i][i] is zero because a single matrix needs no multiplication. Iterate by chain length.

The time is O(n³) and space is O(n²). A senior nuance is that this is the archetypal interval DP where you choose a split operation, and storing the optimal split index lets you reconstruct the actual parenthesization.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At National Bank of India, a risk engine multiplies a chain of covariance and factor matrices, and the grouping order changes the arithmetic cost by orders of magnitude on large dimensions. This is exactly how Matrix Chain Multiplication works.

Problem 2 — Trying all parenthesizations explicitly is exponential (Catalan numbers). This is exactly why the DP memoizes the best cost of every subchain.

The mini-project builds a `MatrixChainPlanner`, a `BankLogFormatter`, and a runnable demo.

sections.s5_journey:
The input dimensions are forty, twenty, thirty, ten, thirty, describing four matrices.

Step 1: The diagonal is zero because a single matrix needs no multiplication.

Step 2: Length-two chains are computed directly, for example multiplying the forty-by-twenty and twenty-by-thirty matrices costs forty times twenty times thirty.

Step 3: Longer chains try every split point, combining the best left and right subchain costs plus the join cost.

Step 4: The best split for each interval is kept, so costs propagate toward the full chain.

Step 5: The minimum total for the whole chain is twenty-six thousand, and the three-dimension case gives six thousand.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Matrix Chain Multiplication is the archetypal interval dynamic programming problem. Matrix multiplication is associative, so the final product is the same no matter how I group the operations, but the arithmetic cost is very different. If one matrix is a by b and the next is b by c, multiplying them costs a times b times c scalar multiplications, so the grouping order matters enormously.

I define dp of i and j as the minimum cost to multiply the subchain of matrices from i to j. For every split point k inside the interval, the cost is the best cost of the left group, plus the best cost of the right group, plus the cost of multiplying the two resulting matrices, which uses the boundary dimensions. A single matrix needs no multiplication, so the diagonal is zero, and I fill the table by increasing chain length so subchains are ready. The answer covers the whole chain, and I can store the best split index to reconstruct the actual parenthesization.

In my project at National Bank of India, a risk engine multiplied a chain of covariance and factor matrices where the grouping order changed the cost by orders of magnitude on large dimensions. Trying all parenthesizations is exponential because their count follows the Catalan numbers, so I used this cubic-time interval DP that memoizes the best cost of every subchain.
